Similitude
sih-MIL-ih-tude
noun
From the Latin similitudo, likeness, from similis, like. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew temunah (a visible form or shape) and demuth (likeness), and the Greek homoiōma and homoiōsis.

Biblical Definition

A similitude is a likeness — either a visible form seen, or a comparison spoken. Both senses bear great doctrinal weight. Of Moses the LORD said, “With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold” (Num 12:8): a nearness of communion granted to no other prophet, yet still not the naked essence, for no man hath seen God at any time. Over against that singular grant stands the sharpest word in the chapter of the second commandment. At Horeb, “ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice” (Deu 4:12), and therefore, “Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb” (Deu 4:15). The argument is exact and binding: God gave Israel a voice and withheld a shape, so that they should make no shape. Israel broke it at Sinai, and the Psalmist writes the epitaph: “Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass” (Psa 106:20). The spoken sense follows the same rule — God taught by similitudes through the prophets (Hos 12:10), by comparison and figure, which is likeness in words rather than likeness in wood and stone.

Webster 1828 Definition

Likeness; resemblance; a visible form or shape; also a comparison, parable, or figure by which one thing is likened to another.

SIMILITUDE, n. [L. similitudo, from similis, like.] Likeness; resemblance; likeness in nature, qualities or appearance.

A visible form or shape; that which is seen of a thing — “ye saw no manner of similitude” (Deu 4:15).

Comparison; simile; the act of likening one thing to another for instruction.

“I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets” (Hos 12:10).

Of man: made after the similitude of God (Jas 3:9), and therefore not to be cursed.

Key Scripture

Num 12:8 — "With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold: wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?"

Deu 4:12 — "And the LORD spake unto you out of the midst of the fire: ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice."

Deu 4:15 — "Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:"

Psa 106:20 — "Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass."

Modern Corruption

The second commandment’s ground — no similitude was seen, therefore none may be made — is set aside wherever images of God and of Christ are venerated, printed, filmed, and hung for devotion.

expand to see more

Rome divided the Decalogue so that the prohibition of images is folded into the first commandment and effectively lost, and the Second Council of Nicaea (787) licensed the veneration of images with a distinction between latria and dulia that Deu 4:15 never grants. The Eastern churches went further and made the icon a channel of devotion. But Moses’ argument is not about the crudeness of the image; it is about the mode of revelation. God came in fire and gave a voice and withheld a shape, on purpose, that His people might worship by hearing and not by seeing. Israel’s first great apostasy was not a denial of the LORD but an image of Him — a calf, hailed as the god that brought them up out of Egypt — and the Psalmist calls that exchange the loss of their glory (Psa 106:20). The Reformed churches recovered the point: the regulative principle of worship follows straight out of Deu 4, and the 1689 Confession forbids the worship of God by images or any other way not prescribed in Holy Scripture.

The modern form is softer and nearly universal. Few Protestants bow to a statue, but the pictured Christ hangs in nurseries, fills flannelgraphs, and walks through films with an actor’s face; and the image, not the text, becomes the mental furniture of the congregation’s piety. It will not do to answer that Christ has a true human nature and may therefore be pictured, for His Person is not divisible: what is depicted is either less than He is or a lie about Him. The Puritans pressed exactly this, and their conclusion deserves a hearing rather than a shrug. Recover the ordinance God actually gave. Faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Rom 10:17); the preached Word, the read Word, and the two visible signs Christ Himself instituted are the appointed helps. And note the one similitude Scripture does command us to honour: man himself, made after the similitude of God (Jas 3:9), whom we are forbidden to curse.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin similitudo, likeness; Hebrew temunah, a visible form — the very thing Israel was not shown.

expand to see more

Similitude — Latin similitudo, from similis, like.

Hebrew temunah (H8544), a visible form or shape (Deu 4:12, 15; Num 12:8).

Hebrew demuth (H1823), likeness — the word of Gen 1:26.

Greek homoiōma / homoiōsis, likeness (Rom 5:14; Jas 3:9).

Second sense: a spoken comparison or figure, the prophets’ teaching method (Hos 12:10).

Usage

"Deu 4:12–15 is the ground of the second commandment: a voice was given, a shape withheld."

"Moses beheld the similitude of the LORD by singular grace; it was never a warrant for images."

"Psa 106:20 names image-making an exchange of glory, not a devotional aid."
